title: Milestone: How Markets Work
objective: After this level you can connect money, banks, investing and markets into one picture of how an economy runs.
summary: Prices are messages that tell people what's scarce, with nobody giving orders. Money makes them readable, and supply and demand run markets for goods, work and savings alike.

cards.headline: Milestone: halfway to Mastery. Time to see the whole machine.
cards.body: Money, markets, supply, demand, competition, incentives, scarcity. They aren't separate topics. They're one machine, and the price tag is where every part of it meets.

cards.headline: Prices are messages
cards.body: In 1945, economist Friedrich Hayek asked you to imagine tin becoming scarcer, from a new use or a lost source. Tin users don't need to know which. The price rises, and they economize. Hayek called the price system a mechanism for communicating information: it gets tens of thousands of strangers to use a material more sparingly, with nobody giving orders.

cards.headline: Money makes the message readable
cards.body: Those messages need Level 1's money. As a unit of account, it puts every price on one ruler, so tin, bread and a haircut can be compared at a glance. Radford's camp showed it in miniature: once prices were quoted in cigarettes, like cheese for seven, anyone could compare anything with anything.

cards.headline: One machine, many markets
cards.body: The same machine runs markets you've met elsewhere in this tree. In labor markets, job seekers supply work and employers demand it. In financial markets, savers supply money and borrowers demand it, and they meet at a rate of return, like an interest rate. Banks, shares and paychecks have their own chapters, but underneath it's supply and demand, meeting at a price.

mascot.line: This is Level 44's scissors again, cutting in every market.

cards.headline: Milestone: markets mapped
learned: How prices carry messages about what's scarce, so strangers adjust without anyone giving orders.
Why supply and demand, like two scissor blades, push a price toward the point where they meet.
Why a legal price floor creates a surplus and a legal price ceiling creates a shortage.
How competition keeps prices down, and why a monopoly sells less at a higher price.

questions.prompt: From Level 41: which of these counts as a market?

options.label: Only a building with stalls
options.rationale: A market needs no building.

options.label: Only a government price list
options.rationale: A price list is not a meeting of buyers and sellers.

options.label: Only trades paid in cash
options.rationale: Markets work with any kind of payment, or through go-betweens.

options.label: Any way buyers and sellers get in contact, even a website

questions.explanation: A market is any means by which buyers and sellers get in contact to trade. It need not be a place.

questions.prompt: In Hayek's tin example, what tells tin users to use less tin?

options.label: An order from the government
options.rationale: Nobody gives orders: that is the point.

options.label: A rise in the price of tin
A report explaining where the tin went
options.rationale: Users don't need to know why tin is scarcer.

options.label: A fall in the price of tin
options.rationale: A falling price would tell them to use more.

questions.explanation: The rising price carries the message that tin is scarcer, so users economize without knowing the cause.

questions.prompt: A frost destroys part of the orange crop. Using Levels 42 and 44, what happens to the price of oranges?

options.label: Supply falls, a shortage opens, and the price rises
Demand falls, so the price drops
options.rationale: The frost hits growers, not buyers.

options.label: Nothing, because only price can change supply
options.rationale: Weather shifts the whole supply curve.

options.label: Supply rises, so the price drops
options.rationale: Frost cuts supply; it does not raise it.

questions.explanation: Weather shifts supply down. At the old price buyers want more than there is, so sellers raise the price.

questions.prompt: Why can a monopoly set a higher price than a firm in a competitive market?

options.label: Its costs are always higher
options.rationale: It's about rivals, not costs.

options.label: The law requires monopolies to charge more
options.rationale: No law sets its price; nothing stops it.

options.label: It has no rivals selling a substitute
Its buyers are richer
options.rationale: Buyers are the same; the missing rivals are the difference.

questions.explanation: A monopoly has no substitute competing with it and barriers keep rivals out, so it can set its price without fear of competition.

questions.prompt: What lesson do Hanoi's rat bounty and Europe's butter mountains share?

options.label: Governments should never pay anyone for anything
options.rationale: Too sweeping: the lesson is about what gets rewarded.

options.label: People respond to rewards, even ones that backfire
Shortages always follow a bounty
options.rationale: Both stories ended with too much, not too little.

options.label: Markets ignore government rules
options.rationale: Both rules changed behavior a lot; that's the problem.

questions.explanation: Paying for tails produced rat farms; paying high farm prices produced mountains of butter. People respond to incentives.

questions.prompt: Which of Level 1's three jobs of money lets a price act as a message everyone can read?

options.label: Store of value
options.rationale: That is money keeping its worth until later.

options.label: Medium of exchange
options.rationale: That is money being passed along as payment.

options.label: Unit of account
Double coincidence of wants
options.rationale: That's barter's matching problem, not a job of money.

questions.explanation: As a unit of account, money puts every price on one ruler, so anyone can compare one price with another.

questions.prompt: From Level 49: why is time called the ultimate scarce resource?

options.label: It can be bought only by the rich
options.rationale: Nobody can buy extra time.

options.label: Everyone, rich or poor, has the same 24 hours a day
Clocks are expensive to make
options.rationale: Scarcity is about wants beating what is available.

options.label: Governments ration it by law
options.rationale: No law is involved; the day simply has 24 hours.

questions.explanation: Scarcity touches everyone: however rich you are, the day still has 24 hours.
